extracted.intended_audience: researchers and academics who perform peer review for journals and conferences
extracted.subtask_short: writing peer reviews for academic journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researchers on what makes a good or bad peer review when evaluating manuscripts; includes behavioral, structural, and language-based criteria to produce constructive reviews. Applies to reviewers preparing reports for journal editors and authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-objective
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a characteristic of bad reviews: indicates reviewer bias or lack of impartial assessment. Anti-patterns: judgments based on personal preference rather than evidence from the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-organized
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-organized
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bad review trait: lack of structure makes it hard for authors to follow or identify priorities. Anti-patterns: stream-of-consciousness notes, unordered lists of concerns without headings or grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-instructional or informative
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-instructional or informative
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bad review trait: provides criticism without actionable information. Examples include vague complaints that do not help authors improve the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fails to identify major flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: Fails to identify major flaws
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad reviews may miss substantive problems in methodology, interpretation, or results. Guidance: identify and explain major flaws clearly and with evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fails to communicate criticism so authors can improve
rubrics_metrics.description: Fails to communicate criticism so authors can improve
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bad review may point out problems but not explain how to address them. Good practice: pair criticism with concrete suggestions for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague, unhelpful summary statements
rubrics_metrics.description: "The paper is not good. The authors should have done a better job." — vague, doesn't help improve
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid one-line global judgments. Instead, specify why the paper is inadequate and what concrete changes are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexplained critiques (non-actionable comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Figure 3 is not clear" — without explaining why or how to improve
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When flagging clarity issues, explain what is unclear and propose how to fix it (e.g., redraw figure, add labels, clarify caption, provide additional data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insulting or unprofessional language
rubrics_metrics.description: Insulting or unprofessional language
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never use rude or abusive phrasing. Editors should remove such comments before sending to authors. Maintain respectful tone even when criticizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unstructured stream of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Unstructured stream of consciousness listing many concerns without indicating which are most serious
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize concerns and indicate priority/importance. Number or label major vs minor issues to help authors and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviews that are too short
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews that are too short (one or two sentences)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extremely brief reviews rarely provide sufficient evidence or actionable feedback. Provide a summary, evidence for judgments, and concrete guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviews that focus only on grammar/typos
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews that focus only on grammar/typos and miss substantive issues
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While language issues matter, ensure the review engages with the scientific/technical substance (methods, results, interpretation) rather than only surface errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviews that demand citations of the reviewer's own work
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews that demand citations of the reviewer's own work
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid self-serving demands to cite the reviewer's publications. Recommend citations only when genuinely relevant and unbiased; declare conflicts when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviews that are factually wrong about the paper's claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews that are factually wrong about the paper's claims
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure factual accuracy when summarizing or critiquing the manuscript. Check the paper carefully before asserting that it claims X or fails to show Y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polite, honest and clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Polite, honest and clear to the authors
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be courteous and straightforward. Honesty about quality is important but should be expressed respectfully and with clarity to enable improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write clearly for non-native English readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Write clearly to be understood by people whose native language is not English
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use straightforward language, avoid idioms or culturally specific phrasing, and structure sentences to aid comprehension for international authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review as if it were your own work
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the author's work as if it was their own
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a constructive mindset aimed at improving the manuscript rather than merely judging it; think about how you'd address the issues if you were the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use constructive, specific language
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive Language Examples (e.g., prefer citing prior work specifically rather than vague claims)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Instead of 'This problem has been solved by many people years ago', give precise citations and explain differences: 'This problem has been solved by A. Smith (AI Journal, 1992), with improvements by C. Miller (ECAI, 1999)'. Use specific alternatives and citations to support statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced evaluation of merits and shortcomings
rubrics_metrics.description: Offers a balanced evaluation highlighting both merits and shortcomings
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out strengths as well as weaknesses to provide a fair assessment and guide improvement; avoid only negative or only positive focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pair constructive criticism with positive feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Pairs constructive criticism with positive feedback
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When noting problems, also acknowledge what works well. This helps authors understand priorities and preserves morale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer to specific examples with line numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to specific examples with line numbers when possible
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite exact locations (page/line/figure) to make it easy for authors to find the issue; increases verifiability of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish major from minor concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes major from minor concerns
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly separate flaws that affect validity or conclusions from minor issues (presentation, typos). Number or label major concerns to indicate priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest concrete improvements, not just criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggests concrete improvements, not just criticism
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer actionable recommendations (e.g., additional analyses, alternative interpretations, reorganization) rather than only pointing out problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make claims verifiable from the manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Makes claims that are verifiable from the manuscript text
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base critiques on evidence in the paper; avoid speculation about authors' intentions and ensure criticisms can be checked against the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge what the authors got right
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledges what the authors got right
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly note valid methods, important contributions, or clear explanations to provide a balanced view and help editors weigh the manuscript's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with the substance rather than the surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Engages with the substance rather than the surface
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on methodological rigor, interpretation, novelty, and contribution instead of only formatting or minor editorial issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary paragraph demonstrating comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary paragraph demonstrating comprehension
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin the review with a concise summary of the paper's aim, methods, and conclusions to show you understood the manuscript; this orients editors and authors to your perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengths section with specific positives
rubrics_metrics.description: Strengths section with specific positives
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List clear, specific strengths of the manuscript (novelty, thoroughness, clear writing) to balance criticism and indicate value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major concerns numbered and ordered by importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Major concerns numbered, ordered by importance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number and prioritize major issues so authors know what to address first; explain why each is important and what impact it has on conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor concerns for clarity, typos, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor concerns for clarity, typos, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect smaller issues (writing, formatting, minor clarifications) in a separate section so they don't obscure major methodological points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation with clear justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation with clear justification
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear recommendation to the editor (accept, revise, reject) and justify it based on evidence and the balance of major/minor concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: respectful, constructive, professional
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone: respectful, constructive, professional
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain professionalism throughout; avoid sarcasm, insults, or hostile language. Constructive tone helps authors respond productively and aids editors in mediation.
